#### Three Formalizations

Consider the language `L` of possibly empty strings over the symbols `a, b, c` where the first `a` precedes the first `b`.

1. Give a regular grammar that generates `L`.

Right-linear regular grammar with start symbol `S`:

```
S → ε  |  c S  |  a T
T → ε  |  a T  |  b T  |  c T
```

In state `S` we have not yet seen an `a`; we may stay there with `c`s, terminate (giving a `c`-only string), or take an `a` and move to `T`. Once in `T` (the first `a` has been consumed), any subsequent symbol is allowed — every later `b` is safely *after* the first `a`. A leading `b` is impossible because `S` has no `b`-production.

2. Give a regular expression that describes `L`.

`c* (a (a|b|c)*)?`

Reading: zero or more `c`s; then optionally an `a` followed by any combination of `a`, `b`, `c`. The optional second part is exactly the moment the first `a` appears (so any `b` in the string is strictly to its right). Strings of pure `c`s (including $\varepsilon$) match the first factor alone; strings with no `b` and at least one `a` match `c* a (a|c)*`; strings with a `b` must have the `c* a` prefix, so the `b` necessarily appears after the first `a`.

3. Give a finite state automaton that accepts `L`.

A deterministic FSA with three states $q_0$ (start, accepting), $q_1$ (after the first `a`, accepting), and $q_2$ (trap, non-accepting):

```
       c                    a, b, c
       ↺                    ↺
   ┌── q₀ ──a→ q₁ ────────────────→ ⊙
   │   │                     ↑
   │   └──b→ q₂   (trap)
   │
   └── (acc)        q₁ also acc.
```

Tabular form:

| state | a   | b   | c   | accept |
| :---- | :-- | :-- | :-- | :----- |
| q₀    | q₁  | q₂  | q₀  | ✓      |
| q₁    | q₁  | q₁  | q₁  | ✓      |
| q₂    | q₂  | q₂  | q₂  | ✗      |

$q_0$ represents "no `a` seen yet"; on reading `c` we stay in $q_0$; on reading `a` we move to $q_1$; on reading `b` we fall into the trap $q_2$ (because a `b` has appeared before any `a`). From $q_1$ every symbol keeps us in $q_1$. Both $q_0$ and $q_1$ are accepting, so we accept strings that end without ever seeing a "premature" `b`.

This automaton mirrors the regular grammar: $q_0 \leftrightarrow S$, $q_1 \leftrightarrow T$, `q₂ ↔ dead`. It also corresponds line-for-line to the regex `c* (a (a|b|c)*)?` — the `c*` loop is the self-loop at $q_0$, the `a`-transition is the entry to $q_1$, and `(a|b|c)*` is the self-loop at $q_1$.
